title: Name and domain checks are not trademark rights

sources.claim: Registering a business name with a state, a DBA, or a domain name is not the same as trademark rights; trademark protection is a separate process.

sections.skill: Separate name availability from trademark rights

questions.prompt: Nia bought the domain "glowpaws.com." What does this show?

choices.text: That domain was available to buy.
No other business anywhere may use the name "Glow Paws."
The state has approved "Glow Paws" as her legal entity.
She owns the trademark "Glow Paws" everywhere in the country.

questions.correct_answer: That domain was available to buy.
questions.intro: Checking a name is not the same as owning it. A domain name you can buy, a social media handle that is free, or a state's approval of an LLC name only shows that THAT specific spot was available. It does not give trademark rights, and it does not mean the name is safe to use. Another business may already use the same or a similar name for similar goods or services, and could object. Before investing in a name, also search for businesses using it and consider a trademark search (US: the USPTO database). Rules: US, check current guidance.
questions.feedback: Buying a domain only shows that the domain was available.

sections.skill: An empty parking spot is not a deed

questions.prompt: An available domain is most like what?

choices.text: A building permit
An empty parking spot
A signed lease for ten years
A deed to land

questions.correct_answer: An empty parking spot
questions.intro: Finding an empty parking spot means you can park there right now. It does not mean you own the land. Name checks work the same way. An available domain or handle is an empty spot on one website. A state approving your LLC name is an empty spot in that state's list. None of them is a deed that proves you own the name against everyone else. Ownership-like rights to a brand name come from trademark law, which is a separate system.
questions.feedback: It is only availability.
